newsitem.title: ITALY: Tietmeyer says measures for EMU must last - LaStampa.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says measures for EMU must last - LaStampa.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the German central bank was sceptical about "one-off" measures to restore a country's state finances to temporary health in order to gain early access to European economic and monetary union, an article in Turin daily La Stampa said.
"Reducing the deficit just for a year is no use at all," La Stampa quoted Tietmeyer as saying at a meeting with foreign press in Bonn on Thursday.
La Stampa questioned whether this was a direct criticism of the Italian government's so-called "Tax for Europe" as part of its austerity 1997 draft budget.
Tietmeyer has already said he would welcome Italy's participation as a founder member of EMU as long as it met Maastricht Treaty criteria in a lasting way.
According to La Stampa, Tietmeyer said he did not wish to comment on any specific measure. "It is up to Italy to decide how to reduce its deficit in a lasting way.
"But there is a correlation between debt and the public deficit. The higher the debt, the lower the deficit should be.
"I do not want to discuss whether Italy's debt is too high. The Maastricht Treaty lays down that if it exceeds 60 percent of gross domestic product it must come down in an adequate way.
"And this can not be done with one-off measures," Tietmeyer was reported as saying.
Italy's budget, currently going through the lower house of parliament, aims to lop 62.5 trillion lire off next year's projected deficit.
The package includes some 12.5 trillion lire of so-called Treasury operations and some 12.5 trillion lire to be raised by the Europe Tax which the government has yet to detail.
Italy's Treasury ministry has rejected domestic press criticism of creative accounting and financial trickery in order to gain early access to the single European currency.
The government has said it will meet the Maastricht parameter of a deficit to GDP ratio of 3.0 percent next year.

But its targeted debt to GDP ratio for 1997, not taking into account the 25 trillion lire of Treasury and Euro tax measures, stands at 120.6 percent -- almost twice its Maastricht target of 60 percent.
